newsitem.title: USA: Slow-motion flood disaster looms for U.S. plains.
newsitem.headline: Slow-motion flood disaster looms for U.S. plains.

text.p: Flood-weary residents of the northern plains heard the bad news on Friday that high water could persist for weeks as the slow-motion disaster put a strain on temporary flood barriers and on emotions.

"We're looking at a slow continuous melt," Capt. Pat Richards of North Dakota's Emergency Management Division said. "We've been warning people that a lot of reservoirs will have to put out water, so those river levels will likely stay up for quite some time."
"There's so much water that still lies south of Fargo the river will probably be in flood stage at least two to three weeks," geologist Donald Schwert said.
Vice President Al Gore arrived for a quick tour of the three-state flood region, stopping in Watertown, South Dakota, where he commiserated with flood victims.

Even where flooded rivers have receded in western Minnesota, returning residents were confronted with jagged ice filling their homes and freezing their cars in place. Farmers freed livestock trapped as water froze around their legs.
The week of flooding peaked at an historic level in Fargo, where National Guard troops patrolled a makeshift dike of earth and sandbags holding back the cresting Red River.

"We've won the battle so far but we need to continue our efforts," Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness said. "Now the problem becomes one of follow-up and making sure those dikes hold. We are not out of the woods by any means. It may take 10 to 14 days before we really feel safe."

Last weekend's storm that brought rain, ice and a heavy coating of snow hastened the flood disaster, which had been anticipated after the region received double its normal snowfall over the winter. Thousands of people have been driven from their homes.
An offer of free food and beer to those willing to lay sandbags around the Wild Rice bar brought so many volunteers that the tavern cancelled the appeal within 15 minutes.

Nearly a dozen people have died in accidents attributed to snowstorm and flooding. A 17-year-old became the latest death attributed to the flood when he and a friend drove their car around a barricade and slipped into a washed-out culvert.
Elsewhere, tornadoes touched down in northwest Texas on Thursday night, killing one man in the White River area and wrecking several homes in Lubbock.
